c.tagline: Glamorous Costa del Sol resort town of yacht marinas, sun-soaked beaches, and whitewashed old-town charm

taxi.fareNote: Official white taxis with a diagonal stripe run regulated meters set by the town hall; fixed fares apply to Málaga airport runs, so confirm the rate before departure

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number covering police, fire, and ambulance; 091 reaches the National Police directly

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Casco Antiguo: Plaza de los Naranjos, the orange-tree-lined old town square
hood_landmark.Puerto Banús: the glitzy superyacht marina lined with designer boutiques
hood_landmark.Golden Mile: the Puente Romano resort and its palm-lined seafront promenade
hood_landmark.Nueva Andalucía: the 'Golf Valley' fairways of Los Naranjos, Las Brisas and Aloha
hood_landmark.San Pedro de Alcántara: the landscaped Boulevard de San Pedro linking town to its beach promenade

avoid.reason: Pickpockets work the old town and Puerto Banús nightlife, and flashy watches and jewellery have attracted targeted thefts around the marina late at night.

hood_desc: Marbella's medieval old town of narrow whitewashed lanes centered on the flower-filled Plaza de los Naranjos. Packed with tapas bars, boutiques, and the town's oldest church, it's the most walkable and historic base.
The famed marina lined with superyachts, designer boutiques, and rooftop clubs that put Marbella on the jet-set map. Nightlife and people-watching here run late and glossy.
A beachfront strip of five-star resorts, private villas, and palm-lined avenues connecting the old town to Puerto Banús. Home to some of Spain's most exclusive hotels.
An inland residential district built around golf courses, popularly nicknamed the 'Golf Valley.' Quiet, leafy, and geared toward longer-stay visitors and expats.
A relaxed seaside town just west of Marbella with a long promenade, family beaches, and a growing food scene, popular with locals seeking a lower-key alternative.
lodging: Hard Rock Hotel Marbella – Puerto Banús
The Westin La Quinta Golf Resort & Spa

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: Cash or card onboard; multi-trip cards available at kiosks
transit.note: No rail or metro; buses run along the coast to San Pedro and Puerto Banús, but most visitors rely on taxis, rideshare, or rental cars

train: No station in Marbella; nearest is Málaga María Zambrano, ~50 km away
bus: Frequent Avanza coaches along the coast to Málaga, Fuengirola, and Estepona

tip.r: Rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants is appreciated but not obligatory; service is not usually included

landmarks: Casco Antiguo (Old Town)
A whitewashed maze of flower-hung lanes, wrought-iron balconies and orange trees that preserves Andalusian charm amid the Costa del Sol glamour.
Plaza de los Naranjos
Marbella's 15th-century Renaissance square, framed by the old town hall and fragrant orange trees, is the postcard heart of the old town.
Puerto Banús
The Mediterranean's flashiest marina lines superyachts, supercars and designer boutiques along a quayside made for unapologetic people-watching.
Avenida del Mar
An elegant pedestrian boulevard linking old town to sea, studded with ten surreal bronze sculptures by Salvador Dalí.
Iglesia Mayor de la Encarnación
A honey-toned 16th-century church whose baroque stone portal and mighty Sol Mayor organ anchor the spiritual life of the old town.
Parque de la Alameda
A shady 18th-century garden of fountains and hand-painted ceramic benches, the perfect pause between old town strolls and the beach.
Paseo Marítimo
Marbella's palm-lined seafront promenade unspools for kilometers past golden beaches and chiringuitos grilling sardine skewers over open fires.
La Concha
The shell-shaped 1,215-meter mountain looming behind Marbella rewards hikers with vertiginous ridgeline views stretching to Gibraltar and Morocco on clear days.
Murallas del Castillo (Arab Castle Walls)
Remnants of Marbella's 10th-century Moorish fortress hide among old-town houses, their rough stone recalling the city's Umayyad origins.
Villa Romana de Río Verde
A seaside 1st-century Roman villa near Puerto Banús preserving playful black-and-white mosaics of kitchenware, sandals and Medusa.

train.note: Marbella has no railway station - the Costa del Sol line stops at Fuengirola, about 30 km east, and a long-promised extension has never been built. Take the Cercanías C-1 from Málaga to Fuengirola and continue by bus, or use the direct coach. Renfe services for the rest of Spain start from Málaga María Zambrano (https://www.renfe.com/es/en).

bus.note: No international coaches start in Marbella. The bus station is on the northern edge of town, with very frequent ALSA (https://www.alsa.com/en) and Avanza services to Málaga (about 45 minutes on the toll road), the airport, Puerto Banús, Estepona and Algeciras for the Morocco ferries. The coach is the standard way in and out.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Marbella - Puerto Banús and the town harbour are yacht marinas. The nearest crossings to Morocco leave from Algeciras and Tarifa, about an hour southwest, and the Melilla ferries sail from Málaga.

half.name: Ronda
half.blurb: A mountain town about an hour away built around a deep gorge, crossed by an 18th-century stone bridge.

half.name: Gibraltar
half.blurb: A British territory about an hour and fifteen minutes away with wild Barbary macaques and views across the strait to Africa.

half.name: Mijas Pueblo
half.blurb: A whitewashed hill village about thirty minutes away with narrow cobbled streets and donkey-taxi rides.
